blocks.name: Read

blocks.text:
The sheet takes its game content (classes, races, spells, items, feats, monsters) from **one of two sources** — both ultimately the 5eTools data set, just delivered differently:

## 1. A `source-data.json` file (Settings → Source books → "Import file…")
This is the portable option. It must be a JSON file produced by the repo's **`build-data.py`**, which extracts and reshapes a local 5eTools `data/` directory into a single file. The importer validates the shape — it has to be an object with at least `races`, `classes`, and `spells` arrays (plus the rest: `feats`, `items`, `monsters`, etc.). Any other JSON is rejected with *"That doesn't look like sourcebook data."*

Generate it like:
```bash
python3 build-data.py            # PHB by default
SOURCE_BOOK=DMG python3 build-data.py   # a specific book
```
It reads from `~/My Drive/5etools/data` (override with the `FIVETOOLS_DATA` env var).

## 2. A running 5eTools server (Settings → Source books → server URL + "Load" / "Load all books")
Point the **server URL** field (default `http://localhost:5050`) at a local 5eTools instance — really any static server serving the 5eTools `data/` JSON tree. The sheet then fetches each book's raw JSON and does the extraction in-browser. This is what supports per-book loading and the stale-data "reload" banner.

## Not a source
The **"Save a copy" `.html`** export and the gitignored **`Character Sheet (Source Data).html`** are full sheets with data already baked into a `<script id="source-data">` block — you open those directly, you don't "point to" them as a source.

So: **a `build-data.py`-generated `source-data.json`**, or **a 5eTools server URL**. Both require you to own/run a 5eTools copy (the content is WotC's and isn't shipped in this repo).

text: What if we want to import a homebrew source?

blocks.name: Read

blocks.text:
Short answer: **there's no first-class homebrew importer today** — but homebrew is very doable, because 5eTools homebrew uses the *same per-entry schema* as official content. The only thing standing in the way is file *layout*, not data format. Here are your options, easiest first.

## What the sheet accepts now
- **`source-data.json`** (Import file…) — must already be in the sheet's *extracted* shape (`races`/`classes`/`spells`/… arrays produced by `build-data.py`).
- **5eTools server** — fetches the standard split layout (`races.json`, `class/index.json` → `class/class-*.json`, `spells/index.json` keyed by source code, etc.).

A 5eTools **brew file** is a single JSON with top-level `class`, `subclass`, `spell`, `race`, `feat`, `item`, `monster`… arrays plus a `_meta.sources` block and its own source code. Neither path reads that layout directly.

## Three ways to get homebrew in

**1. Merge into a `source-data.json` by hand (best for a few things).**
Open a `build-data.py` output, and append your homebrew entries — in the *extracted* schema — into the matching arrays (e.g. a spell needs `{name, level, school, time, range, components, duration, text, higher, ritual, conc, material}`). Reliable for a handful of spells/feats/items; tedious for a whole class.

**2. Fold the brew into your 5eTools `data/` tree, then run `build-data.py`.**
Split the brew's arrays into the official file locations under its source code, add that code to `class/index.json` / `spells/index.json`, then `SOURCE_BOOK=<brewcode> python3 build-data.py`. The entry schema already matches, so extraction "just works" — but the manual splicing/indexing is fiddly.

**3. (Recommended) Add a real "Import homebrew" button.**
The in-browser extractors (`etSpells`, `etClasses`, `etFeats`, item parsers, `etMonsters`…) already take *collections + a source code* and produce the merged shape — exactly what `fetch5etoolsBook` assembles before `mergeBook()`. A homebrew importer would just: read a 5eTools brew `.json`, remap its top-level arrays onto the collections those functions expect, pull the source code from `_meta.sources`, run the same pipeline, and `mergeBook()` it into `DATA` alongside your other books. That gives homebrew the same per-book filtering and stale-data handling as official content.

Option 3 is clean and fits the existing architecture well. Want me to build it — accept a standard 5eTools brew JSON file and merge it in?

text: What if I have a PDF document of homebrew data?

blocks.text:
A PDF is a different situation: it's unstructured prose/tables, not data. The sheet has **no PDF parsing** and never will at runtime — it only ingests structured JSON. So a PDF always needs a **conversion step** first: someone (or something) has to read the homebrew and re-express it as JSON in either the 5eTools brew schema or the sheet's extracted `source-data.json` shape.

That conversion is exactly the kind of thing I can do for you:

## The workflow
1. **You give me the PDF.** I can read it directly (text and tables, and I can interpret images/layout).
2. **I transcribe the homebrew into JSON.** Two target options:
   - **5eTools brew JSON** — most reusable; works with the "Import homebrew" button (if we build option 3 from the last message), and is portable to actual 5eTools.
   - **Direct `source-data.json` (extracted) shape** — fewer moving parts; import works *today* via "Import file…", or I merge it into an existing book file.
3. **You review and import.** I'll flag anything ambiguous rather than guess.

## Honest caveats
- **Accuracy needs a human pass.** PDFs lose structure — multi-column layouts, stat tables, and spell-detail lines (range/components/duration) often get scrambled. I'll do my best and mark uncertain fields, but you should spot-check before trusting a character built on it.
- **Mechanics vs. flavor.** I'll capture the rules the sheet actually uses (hit die, proficiencies, features by level, spell lists, item stats). Pure lore text gets dropped or stuffed into a feature's description.
- **Scope matters.** A few spells/feats/a subclass is quick and high-confidence. A full homebrew class with subclasses, a spell list, and items is doable but more work and more review.
- **One-time, not live.** The output is a file you import; editing the PDF later means re-converting.

If you want, share the PDF (or tell me where it is) and which target you'd prefer — brew JSON or a ready-to-import `source-data.json` — and I'll start the transcription. If you'd also like the in-app **"Import homebrew"** button so brew JSON loads with per-book filtering, I can build that in parallel.
